title: Final criterion (thm:final) and Algorithm 1 give wrong answer when d(p) != d(q)

comments.author: human
comments.body:
Algorithm 1 returns False at line 5 whenever $d(p)\neq d(q)$ (after the plain-majorization check). On the Jonathan–Plenio example $p=(0.4,0.4,0.1,0.1)$, $q=(0.5,0.25,0.25)$ it returns False, but the correct answer is True (catalyst $(0.6,0.4)$). Therefore Theorem `thm:final` is an incorrect necessary-and-sufficient criterion: it misclassifies every trumping pair with $d(p)>d(q)$ that is not already a plain-majorization pair.

The criterion must include the correct unequal-support clause. Empirically on the JP example: conditions (I) [$P_t(p)<P_t(q)$, $t>1$], (II) [$P_t(p)>P_t(q)$, $0<t<1$], (IV) [$H(p)>H(q)$] all HOLD on the nonzero parts, but (III) [$P_t(p)<P_t(q)$, $t<0$] FAILS: e.g. $P_{-1}(p)=25>10=P_{-1}(q)$, $P_{-2}(p)=212.5>36$. So when $d(p)>d(q)$ the negative-order conditions must be omitted (Klimesh 2007 / Turgut 2007). The algorithm must branch on $d(p)=d(q)$ vs $d(p)>d(q)$ rather than returning False.

Note: the necessity proof `prop:nec` is correct only under its hypothesis $q_n>0$; for $t<0$ with $d(p)>d(q)$ the cancellation $P_t(p)\le P_t(q)$ used there is invalid because the two sides sum over different numbers of positive entries — exactly why (III) is not necessary in that regime.
